purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P12–P16. Together with the earlier representative P11 article, these complete the concrete experience family. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Choose the Telling Detail
use_when: An inventory of features leaves a subject interchangeable with many others.
A stock phrase substitutes for observing the relationship that matters.
A detail invites a larger character judgment than its context supports.
mechanisms: Selecting a particular that changes the reader's understanding
Making relationships or contradictions available through action and objects
Testing an inference against known context
not_ideal_when: A vivid incident would receive more attention than the subject's role warrants.
Selecting an isolated gesture would misrepresent the person or withhold a material explanation.
example_user_queries: My character has a detailed description but still feels generic.
I have described every object in the room and it has no distinctive impression.
How do I choose which details deserve attention?
I keep using phrases like the heart of the community instead of observing what happens.
A gesture suggests something interesting but may not prove what I want it to.
Does a detail have to be unusual to be revealing?
My description feels as if I planted symbols for the reader.
How can I replace a stock character description without adding a long biography?
I want to show how a rule is applied differently to different people.
A true detail makes someone look worse when I leave out the surrounding context.

sources.author: Lauren Kessler
sources.title: Character: The beating heart of narrative
sources.inspected_material: Reporting tools to reveal character, including selection from appearance, surroundings, speech, and action; Ask rather than assume, distinguishing reported thought from projection.
sources.supports: Selecting revealing particulars rather than a complete inventory and grounding nonfiction character description in observation or an identified account.
sources.limits: No quoted literary example or source anecdote is reproduced. The committee, phone, and lunchroom situations are hypothetical; their contextual alternatives and stock-description comparisons are original editorial development.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed passages and connected prose make selection, conceptual contrast, and sensory relevance inspectable in context. A separate image or diagram would add little to these particular explanations; no practice is included.

articles.title: Make Abstractions Tangible
use_when: Readers can repeat a general term but cannot recognize it in practice.
People apparently agree while imagining materially different arrangements.
An example is memorable but its relationship to the concept remains unstated.
mechanisms: Connecting a general claim to a concrete instance or consequence
Using contrasts to expose conceptual boundaries
Returning from particulars to a reusable general idea
not_ideal_when: The reader already has a usable instance and another example would repeat it.
A vivid hypothetical or isolated case is being asked to prove frequency, representativeness, or causation.
example_user_queries: People agree with my proposal but seem to mean different things by the same word.
Readers understand the definition but cannot recognize an example.
My explanation never gets beyond general terms like flexibility and accountability.
I added an anecdote and readers still do not see what it illustrates.
How can I show the practical consequence of an abstract idea?
I want to compare two arrangements that share a label but work differently.
My essay has concrete details but I cannot connect them to the main concept.
How do I show where an example stops fitting?
Can one vivid case establish a general claim?
Do I have to remove abstract language after adding examples?

sources.author: Montana State University Writing Center
sources.title: Clear & Concrete Language
sources.inspected_material: Concrete and Abstract Language, including the complementary uses of clarification through particulars and economy through later abstraction.
sources.supports: Moving between concrete and abstract language according to explanatory need rather than treating either level as universally preferable.
sources.limits: No scientific example or grammatical exercise is reproduced. The scheduling and volunteer-work cases are original; no full Williams and Bizup passage has been inspected or attributed.

sources.author: Jyoti Madhusoodanan
sources.title: Using the Ladder of Abstraction to Elevate Science Stories
sources.inspected_material: Reaching the Top and Connecting the Rungs, particularly the first-hand practitioner interviews about connecting particulars to meaning and moving between levels.
sources.supports: Making the relationship between concrete material and a broader idea available rather than accumulating detail without explanatory direction.
sources.limits: The article draws on the craft discussion and practitioner interviews only. It adopts no neuroscience result, source anecdote, universal policy claim, or claim that an illustrative case establishes a general finding.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed passages and connected prose make selection, conceptual contrast, and sensory relevance inspectable in context. A separate image or diagram would add little to these particular explanations; no practice is included.

articles.title: Engage the Relevant Senses
use_when: A scene is visually described but detached from the observer's physical experience.
Sensory adjectives decorate a setting without contributing to its action.
A body's effort, position, or perceptual limits matter to what happens.
mechanisms: Describing an encounter rather than only a visual inventory
Selecting sensations according to observer and situation
Connecting perception to movement and action
not_ideal_when: Sensory expansion would delay a routine transition without adding a relevant experience.
A perception cannot be supported in nonfiction or is unavailable to the scene's viewpoint.
example_user_queries: Readers can picture the room but the scene feels physically flat.
I keep describing what things look like and little else.
How can sensory details contribute to action rather than decorate it?
Do I need all five senses in every scene?
My character is carrying something heavy but the movement feels effortless.
Should I remove every phrase like she felt or he heard?
How can two people notice the same place differently?
The sensory description slows the story and I do not know what to keep.
Can I describe a smell from a photograph of the scene?
I use bodily cues for emotions but they feel generic.

sources.author: University of Michigan Sweetland Center for Writing
sources.title: How Can I Write More Descriptively?
sources.inspected_material: General Considerations on significant aspects and proportionate description, and In Practice on sensory possibilities including sound, touch, temperature, texture, and weight.
sources.supports: Considering sensory information beyond a visual inventory while giving attention according to the passage's significance.
sources.limits: No source example or exercise is reproduced. The article does not adopt a mandatory five-sense formula, a fixed emotional meaning for a bodily cue, or a universal claim about sensory experience.

sources.author: Lauren Kessler
sources.title: Character: The beating heart of narrative
sources.inspected_material: Ask rather than assume, on the distinction between a nonfiction writer's projection and a subject's identified account.
sources.supports: Keeping reported experience distinct from the writer's invented assumptions.
sources.limits: The ferry and audition are explicitly fictional. The comparisons involving photographs, later visits, and viewpoint access are original editorial development rather than claims about an actual crossing or empirical perception research.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed passages and connected prose make selection, conceptual contrast, and sensory relevance inspectable in context. A separate image or diagram would add little to these particular explanations; no practice is included.

articles.title: Use Metaphor to Reveal a Relationship
use_when: A concept needs an intelligible shape rather than another abstract description.
An attractive comparison imports assumptions that do not fit the subject.
A stock or mixed image obscures the particular relationship the writer means.
mechanisms: Identifying the relationship carried by a comparison
Testing borrowed implications against the subject
Using imagery to express a viewpoint as well as a description
not_ideal_when: A direct statement communicates the relationship more clearly.
An analogy is being used as if it established evidence or justified a conclusion by itself.
example_user_queries: My metaphor sounds vivid but does not explain anything.
How do I know whether a comparison fits the idea?
A familiar image seems to make readers assume the wrong thing.
I want a metaphor that shows a relationship rather than just adding decoration.
Can a comparison be useful even if it does not fit every part of the subject?
My paragraph changes between several images and feels confused.
Do I have to replace every familiar metaphor with a new one?
A narrator's comparison may unfairly make one character look hostile.
How can I make an unfamiliar concept easier to grasp without pretending the analogy proves it?
When should I remove a metaphor and say the point directly?

sources.author: Joe Schall, Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences
sources.title: Definitions, Metaphors, Similes, and Analogies
sources.inspected_material: Making Fundamental Comparisons, including implicit and explicit comparisons and the role of audience and context.
sources.supports: Using comparisons to make relationships and concepts more understandable, with audience and context guiding their use.
sources.limits: No scientific example, student essay, introductory historical claim, or source metaphor is adopted. The archive and dinner are original hypothetical examples, and their interpretive comparisons are editorial development.

sources.author: Texas A&M University Writing Center
sources.title: Rhetorical Terms
sources.inspected_material: The Analogy entry, specifically the possible explanatory usefulness and limits of a comparison.
sources.supports: Recognizing that a comparison has limits and cannot account for every feature of its subject.
sources.limits: No source political quotation, categorical claim about refutability, or assertion that metaphor supplies factual evidence is adopted.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons show the relevant metaphor, inference, or change of sentence movement directly. A separate table or graphic would detach the choices from their context; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Remove Explanatory Echoes
use_when: Commentary restates an implication already available in action, dialogue, or an image.
A paragraph keeps certifying that its preceding material means what it appears to mean.
Removing explanation risks losing necessary context or a genuinely new turn of thought.
mechanisms: Comparing the contribution of commentary with the material before it
Separating orienting knowledge from repeated interpretation
Retaining explanation that adds reasoning, contradiction, or voice
not_ideal_when: The reader lacks the knowledge needed to make the intended inference.
Commentary develops a new thought, a necessary argument connection, or an intentional narrative voice.
example_user_queries: I show an action and then explain what it means in the next sentence.
My editor says I overinterpret every emotional moment.
How can I trust the reader without making the scene confusing?
Does this thought add something or just explain the gesture again?
I am unsure whether the reader knows enough to make the inference.
A cut makes the scene quieter but also removes the character's contradiction.
Should I remove direct statements of emotion from my narration?
My essay repeats an interpretation immediately after making it.
How do I distinguish necessary analysis from explaining the obvious?
The meaning is obvious to me because I know the whole backstory.

sources.author: The Editorial Department
sources.title: Part III: Showing vs. Telling
sources.inspected_material: The opening qualification about leaving too much out and the discussion of redundant interior explanation after dialogue and action, including the editors' use of resist the urge to explain.
sources.supports: Checking whether explicit commentary weakens or restates what a passage already conveys, without treating omission as universally preferable.
sources.limits: No source fictional passage or book excerpt is reproduced. Cora's arrival, contextual alternatives, and narration comparisons are original; no full Self-Editing for Fiction Writers passage review is claimed.

sources.author: Harvard College Writing Center
sources.title: Anatomy of a Body Paragraph
sources.inspected_material: The Evidence and Analysis discussion, especially the need to explain how evidence supports the claim.
sources.supports: Distinguishing necessary interpretive reasoning in an argument from a repeated conclusion.
sources.limits: The theatre survey is hypothetical. Its timeline, contractual context, qualification, and comparisons are original; no source essay example is reproduced.
